title: Smart Cities
description: A radio introduction to smart cities, a discussion between a council officer and a resident, an interview with an engineer and a lecture on the risks of smart technology.
instructions: Read the questions for each part first. Then press Play and listen. Choose the best answer for each question.

parts.title: Part 1 · Radio feature: What is a smart city?
parts.intro: You will hear a radio presenter introducing a programme about smart cities.

script.speaker: Presenter
script.text: Good evening. Imagine a city where the traffic lights change according to how many cars are waiting, where bins send a message when they are full, and where your phone tells you the exact minute the next bus will arrive. This is the idea of a smart city.

script.speaker: Presenter
script.text: The basic principle is simple. Thousands of small sensors collect information about the city, such as traffic, air quality and energy use. Computers then analyse the data to help the city run more efficiently.

script.speaker: Presenter
script.text: The results can be impressive. In one coastal city, sensors in the road told drivers where to find empty parking spaces, and the time spent searching fell by almost a third. Fewer cars driving in circles meant cleaner air as well.

script.speaker: Presenter
script.text: But a smart city isn't only about technology. Experts say that the most successful projects begin with a problem that people actually have, not with a clever gadget looking for a use.

script.speaker: Presenter
script.text: Not everyone is enthusiastic, though. Some residents worry about being watched, and others ask who owns all the information that is gathered. We'll come back to those concerns later in the programme.

script.speaker: Presenter
script.text: First, we go to a town hall, where a council officer is meeting a resident to discuss a new project.

parts.title: Part 2 · A council officer and a resident
parts.intro: You will hear a council officer, Mr Evans, talking to a resident, Mrs Lan, about a smart lighting project.

script.speaker: Evans
script.text: Thank you for coming, Mrs Lan. As you know, we plan to replace the street lights in your area with smart ones. They'll be dimmer when no one is around and brighter when someone walks past.

script.speaker: Lan
script.text: I see. But I'm a bit worried about that. My street is quiet at night, and if the lights are dim I'll feel less safe walking home.

script.speaker: Evans
script.text: I understand that completely. In fact, the lights will stay at about half brightness all night, so they never go dark. And they brighten when they detect movement, which should make people feel safer, not less safe.

script.speaker: Lan
script.text: That sounds better. And what are the benefits for the council? Is it just about saving money?

script.speaker: Evans
script.text: Money is part of it. The new lights use about sixty per cent less electricity, and they report faults by themselves, so we don't need to wait for a resident to phone and complain.

script.speaker: Lan
script.text: Do the lights have cameras? Somebody told me they record people.

script.speaker: Evans
script.text: No, there are no cameras. The sensors only detect movement and count how many people pass. They can't identify anyone, and the information is deleted after a week.

script.speaker: Lan
script.text: Good. I would object if there were cameras. Where will you start?

script.speaker: Evans
script.text: We'll begin in your street and the two streets next to it, partly because the old lights there are the oldest. Work starts in March and should be finished within six weeks.

script.speaker: Lan
script.text: Right. May I come to the next information evening? I'd like to hear from my neighbours too.

parts.title: Part 3 · Interview with a transport engineer
parts.intro: You will hear a presenter, Linh, interviewing a transport engineer, Dr Tom Reed.

script.speaker: Linh
script.text: Dr Reed, your team has been working on reducing traffic in a large city. What was the main idea?

script.speaker: Tom
script.text: We started by asking why people drive to the centre. We discovered that many of them weren't going anywhere important. They simply thought the bus would be unreliable, so they didn't try it.

script.speaker: Linh
script.text: So the problem was trust, not the buses themselves?

script.speaker: Tom
script.text: Largely, yes. Our solution was to give every bus a tracker, and show the real arrival time on a screen at the stop and in an app. Once passengers could see exactly when the bus would arrive, the waiting felt shorter and more people used it.

script.speaker: Linh
script.text: That sounds almost too simple.

script.speaker: Tom
script.text: Sometimes the best technology is simple. We also changed the traffic lights so that buses got a green light slightly earlier. That saved each bus about two minutes on a typical route.

script.speaker: Linh
script.text: Were there any unexpected effects?

script.speaker: Tom
script.text: One, yes. Car drivers complained, because they felt the buses had an unfair advantage. We needed several public meetings to explain that if even a few drivers changed to the bus, the road would be clearer for everyone.

script.speaker: Linh
script.text: Has it worked?

script.speaker: Tom
script.text: After two years, bus use is up by about a fifth, and journey times for cars have not become longer. It isn't a miracle, but it's progress, and the people who live there say the centre feels quieter.

parts.title: Part 4 · Lecture: The risks of smart technology
parts.intro: You will hear a university lecturer, Dr Mai Tran, talking about the problems of smart cities.

script.speaker: Mai
script.text: So far in this course we've looked at the advantages of smart cities. Today I want to be a little critical and discuss three risks.

script.speaker: Mai
script.text: The first is privacy. Even when individual information is anonymous, combining different sets of data can reveal who someone is. For example, if you know where one phone travels each morning and evening, it's not difficult to guess where its owner lives and works.

script.speaker: Mai
script.text: The second risk is security. A city that relies on networked systems can be attacked. Imagine a hacker who gets control of traffic lights or the water supply. Cities need to protect these systems as carefully as they protect their bridges and roads.

script.speaker: Mai
script.text: The third risk is inequality. Smart projects often begin in wealthy areas, where there is already good internet access. If poorer districts are left behind, the gap between them can grow wider, and the people who most need better services get the least.

script.speaker: Mai
script.text: Does this mean smart cities are a bad idea? Not at all. Technology is a tool, and its value depends on how we use it. A well-run project asks residents what they want, publishes clear rules about how data is used, and checks that every neighbourhood benefits.

script.speaker: Mai
script.text: My own view is that the real test of a smart city isn't how many sensors it has, but whether life becomes easier and fairer for ordinary people.

script.speaker: Mai
script.text: For the seminar next week, please read the case study on the course page and prepare two questions you would ask a city mayor.

questions.text: What do the sensors in a smart city collect?
options: Information about traffic, air quality and energy use
Information about shop prices, noise levels and weather forecasts
Information about drivers' spending, parking fines and bus fares
questions.explanation: The presenter says sensors collect information about traffic, air quality and energy use.

evidence.quote: traffic, air quality and energy use

questions.text: What happened in the coastal city with parking sensors?
options: Cars were banned from the centre, so the air became cleaner
Time spent searching for parking fell by almost a third
Parking became free after sensors were fitted in the road
questions.explanation: Searching time fell by almost a third.

evidence.quote: the time spent searching fell by almost a third

questions.text: What do experts say about successful smart projects?
options: They start from a real problem that people have
They need as many sensors as the budget allows
They begin with a clever gadget and then find a use
questions.explanation: Successful projects begin with a problem people actually have.

evidence.quote: begin with a problem that people actually have

questions.text: Why are some residents not enthusiastic?
options: They think the technology is too slow to be useful
They worry about being watched and who owns the data
They believe the new buses will be unreliable and late
questions.explanation: Some worry about being watched and who owns the information.

evidence.quote: Some residents worry about being watched

questions.text: Why does the presenter go to a town hall?
options: To hear a council officer and a resident discuss a project
To interview the mayor about the new town hall budget
To announce the results of a survey about parking spaces
questions.explanation: He introduces a meeting between a council officer and a resident.

evidence.quote: a council officer is meeting a resident

questions.text: Why is Mrs Lan worried at first?
options: She dislikes any kind of change to her street
She fears she will feel less safe in dim streets
She thinks smart lights will cost residents too much
questions.explanation: She says dim lights would make her feel less safe walking home.

evidence.quote: I'll feel less safe walking home

questions.text: How do the new lights behave at night?
options: They are switched off completely when nobody is around
They stay fully bright all night, whether or not anyone passes
They stay at half brightness and brighten when someone passes
questions.explanation: The lights stay at about half brightness and brighten with movement.

evidence.quote: they brighten when they detect movement

questions.text: What are the benefits for the council?
options: Lower electricity use and automatic fault reports
Higher taxes and more income from parking charges
More cameras and faster complaints from residents
questions.explanation: The lights use sixty per cent less electricity and report faults themselves.

evidence.quote: they report faults by themselves

questions.text: What does Mr Evans say about the sensors?
options: They record people's faces and keep the pictures for a week
They only detect movement and the data is deleted after a week
They count passers-by and store the data for a whole year
questions.explanation: There are no cameras, and the information is deleted after a week.

evidence.quote: the information is deleted after a week

questions.text: Why does Mrs Lan want to come to the next information evening?
options: To complain to the council about the cost of the project
To hear the opinions of her neighbours
To vote on whether the new lights should be installed
questions.explanation: She says she would like to hear from her neighbours too.

evidence.quote: I'd like to hear from my neighbours too

questions.text: Why did many people drive to the centre?
options: They believed the bus would be unreliable
They were all going somewhere important in the centre
They found parking in the centre cheap and easy
questions.explanation: They thought the bus would be unreliable and so did not try it.

evidence.quote: They simply thought the bus would be unreliable

questions.text: What was the main solution?
options: Showing real arrival times on screens and in an app
Building new roads so that buses could avoid traffic
Making bus tickets free for everyone living nearby
questions.explanation: Buses got trackers and the real arrival time was shown at stops and in an app.

evidence.quote: show the real arrival time on a screen at the stop and in an app

questions.text: What does Dr Reed say about simple technology?
options: It is too cheap to be taken seriously
Sometimes the best technology is simple
It is never enough without expensive equipment
questions.explanation: He says sometimes the best technology is simple.

evidence.quote: Sometimes the best technology is simple.

questions.text: Why did car drivers complain?
options: The new buses were noisy and polluted the centre
They felt buses had an unfair advantage
Their journey times became longer than before
questions.explanation: They felt the buses had an unfair advantage.

evidence.quote: they felt the buses had an unfair advantage

questions.text: What is Dr Reed's conclusion about the project?
options: It is not a miracle but it is progress
It solved every problem the city had
It failed because few people used the buses
questions.explanation: Bus use is up by about a fifth and car journeys are no longer; he calls it progress, not a miracle.

evidence.quote: It isn't a miracle, but it's progress

questions.text: Why can anonymous data still be a privacy risk?
options: Phones can never be made fully anonymous
Combining data sets can reveal who someone is
Anonymous data is usually published for everyone
questions.explanation: Combining data, such as a phone's daily route, can reveal where someone lives and works.

evidence.quote: combining different sets of data can reveal who someone is

questions.text: What is the second risk?
options: The cost of installing so many cameras
Noise from the sensors in busy streets
Security: networked systems can be attacked
questions.explanation: A city relying on networked systems could be attacked by hackers.

evidence.quote: A city that relies on networked systems can be attacked

questions.text: What does Dr Tran fear about inequality?
options: Internet access will become too expensive for everyone
Wealthy people will move out of the city centre
Poorer districts may be left behind
questions.explanation: If poorer districts are left behind, the gap can grow wider.

evidence.quote: the gap between them can grow wider

questions.text: What is her overall view of smart cities?
options: They are useful tools if used fairly and openly
They are perfect solutions to every urban problem
They are a bad idea because of the risks
questions.explanation: She says smart cities are not a bad idea; value depends on how they are used.

evidence.quote: Technology is a tool

questions.text: What does she mean by the "real test" of a smart city?
options: Whether life becomes easier and fairer for ordinary people
How much money it saves the city each year
How many sensors it has installed in the streets
questions.explanation: She says the test is not the number of sensors but whether life improves for people.

evidence.quote: whether life becomes easier and fairer for ordinary people
